lessons.title: Linguistic diversity and dialects
lessons.anelcac: Notions of linguistic diversity, dialects, names of languages, geographical classification
objectives: Becoming aware of the linguistic diversity of Cameroon (about 280 languages according to the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas)
Distinguish language, dialect and variant according to academic definitions
Naming Bàsàa and locating it in the geographical classification of the languages of Cameroon
Adopt an attitude of respect towards all languages

teacher.intro: Lesson: Linguistic diversity and dialects. Module: Module I — Cameroonian linguistic diversity.
steps: **Setting the context:** Display the map of the Linguistic Mini-Atlas of Cameroon. Ask students which languages are spoken in their family.
**Exploration:** Have students read the definitions in the Mini-Atlas (language, dialect, patois, national language). Locate Bàsàa in its linguistic region.
**Conceptualisation:** Explain the language / dialect distinction with examples: the Bulu, Ewondo, Eton and Mangisa dialects all belong to the Beti-Fang language (Mini-Atlas).
**Application:** Complete a table: name of the language, family, main region, ISO code.
**Assessment:** Each student gives an oral presentation of Bàsàa, indicating family and region.
teacher.freedom: The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas (2013) distinguishes about 280 living languages in Cameroon. The exact number varies according to the criteria (SIL: 274, Ethnologue: 279). Value all the languages cited.
teacher.tips: The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas (2013) distinguishes about 280 living languages in Cameroon. The exact number varies according to the criteria (SIL: 274, Ethnologue: 279). Value all the languages cited.

student.intro: Cameroon is one of the richest nations in the world in languages — the linguistic Mini-Atlas lists about 280! In this lesson, you discover the place of Bàsàa in this great family.
activities: Look at the Mini-Atlas map and find the area where Bàsàa is mainly spoken.
Copy and complete: Bàsàa belongs to the ___ family. It is mostly spoken in the ___ region.
According to the Mini-Atlas, how many living languages are there in the Bàsàa region? Note down this number.
Survey: ask an adult the name of the language in which they were raised and where it is spoken.
Memorise: **dialect** = an intelligible variant of the same language; **national language** = language of an ethnic group that does not extend beyond the borders of one State (ACA LAN).
student.memo: Cameroon has about **280 languages** according to the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas. Bàsàa belongs to a Cameroonian language family and has its own dialectal variants. According to the ACA LAN, a national language is the language of an ethnic group that does not extend beyond the borders of one State.

lessons.title: Classification of languages and linguistic atlas
lessons.anelcac: Classification of the languages of Cameroon: linguistic areas, families, ALCAM atlas
objectives: Name the main linguistic areas of Cameroon
Read and interpret an extract from a linguistic atlas (ALCAM / Mini-Atlas)
Classify Bàsàa according to its typological criteria
Producing a short text presenting Bàsàa

teacher.intro: Lesson: Classification of languages and linguistic atlas. Module: Module I — Cameroonian linguistic diversity.
steps: **Setting the context:** Go back over the definitions. How many language families do students remember?
**Presentation:** The 8 world language families according to Ethnologue (Niger-Kordofanian, Nilo-Saharan, Afro-Asiatic…). Place Cameroonian languages within this whole.
**Explanation:** Show how to find Bàsàa in the ALCAM: ISO code, family, location.
**Guided practice:** In pairs, students find 3 languages neighbouring Bàsàa and note their ISO codes.
**Production:** 5-line paragraph presenting Bàsàa (family, region, speakers, distinctive feature).
teacher.freedom: The online ALCAM is on the Mozilla Data Collective. The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas covers all the administrative regions with maps and statistics.
teacher.tips: The online ALCAM is on the Mozilla Data Collective. The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas covers all the administrative regions with maps and statistics.

student.intro: A linguistic atlas is a specialised map. The ALCAM (Atlas of the Languages of Cameroon) and the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas let you locate Bàsàa precisely.
activities: On the Mini-Atlas map, locate Bàsàa and note its administrative region.
List 3 languages whose area is adjacent to that of Bàsàa.
Classify these 4 languages in a table: Language | Family | Main region.
Write an introductory paragraph about Bàsàa with at least 5 pieces of information taken from the atlas.
Memorise: **ISO 639** = international language codes; **ALCAM** = Atlas des Langues du Cameroun.
student.memo: The **ALCAM** and the **LACAGEO Mini-Atlas** list and locate all the national languages of Cameroon. Cameroon has 8 main language families. Bàsàa appears there with its family and its location. Knowing how to read a linguistic atlas is reading the history of peoples.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants
lessons.title: Vowels of Bàsàa
lessons.anelcac: AGLC vowels — simple, specific, complex
objectives: Identify the simple vowels of the phonological system of Bàsàa
Recognising specific vowels absent from French
Pronouncing vowels correctly in the context of a word
Transcribing words containing vowels according to AGLC

teacher.intro: Lesson: Bàsàa vowels. Module: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write known words in Bàsàa on the board and ask which sounds students hear.
**Presentation:** Introduce the AGLC. Write the simple vowels of Bàsàa on the board, articulating them clearly.
**Explanation:** Vowels specific to Bàsàa that are absent from French (nasal, particular openness…). Listening and repetition exercises.
**Application:** List of 10 words — students underline the vowels and indicate: simple or specific.
**Assessment:** Dictation of 5 simple words — students transcribe them with the correct vowels.
teacher.freedom: Use the examples from the platform's ALCAM vocabulary. For each specific vowel, give a memorable key word.
teacher.tips: Use the examples from the platform's ALCAM vocabulary. For each specific vowel, give a memorable key word.

student.intro: Every language has its own sounds. In Bàsàa, some vowels do not exist in French. This lesson teaches you to hear, pronounce and write them.
activities: Listen to the recordings of the Bàsàa vocabulary and identify the vowels you hear.
Classify the vowels: **Shared with French** | **Specific to Bàsàa**.
Transcribe the 5 dictated words, taking care to note each vowel correctly.
Find 3 words in Bàsàa for each specific vowel and write them down.
Memorise: **AGLC** = Alphabet Général des Langues Camerounaises, the official reference.
student.memo: The vowel system of **Bàsàa** includes simple vowels and specific vowels (e.g. nasalised vowels). They are written using the **AGLC**. Mastery of vowels is the basis of reading and writing in Bàsàa.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants
lessons.title: Bàsàa consonants and written production
lessons.anelcac: Consonants — simple, specific, complex; written production of vowels and consonants
objectives: Identify the consonant system of Bàsàa
Recognising specific consonants absent from French
Articulate consonants correctly in context
Writing words with vowels and consonants correctly notated

teacher.intro: Lesson: Bàsàa consonants and written production. Module: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants.
steps: **Setting the context:** Recall the vowels. What is a consonant?
**Presentation:** Table of Bàsàa consonants according to the AGLC. Stress the specific consonants (labio-velars, prenasalised, implosives…).
**Explanation:** Articulating difficult consonants: in isolation → syllable → word.
**Application:** Minimal pairs: listening to words that differ only by one consonant.
**Production:** 5 simple sentences in Bàsàa with careful consonant transcription.
teacher.freedom: Implosive and prenasalised consonants are often the most difficult for students who learned to read and write in French. Repeat the listening activities many times.
teacher.tips: Implosive and prenasalised consonants are often the most difficult for students who learned to read and write in French. Repeat the listening activities many times.

student.intro: After the vowels, here are the consonants of Bàsàa! Some are unique — you will only hear them in Bàsàa and in a few neighbouring African languages.
activities: Listen to the minimal pairs and tick the word you hear (e.g. bìlí / pìlí).
Transcribe 5 dictated words, paying attention to the specific consonants.
Find in the vocabulary all the words containing a prenasalised consonant. How many do you find?
Compose 3 simple sentences in Bàsàa, each with at least one specific consonant.
Memorise: **minimal pair** = two words identical except for one phoneme.
student.memo: The consonant system of **Bàsàa** includes consonants shared with French and specific consonants (implosives, prenasalised, labio-velars…). Writing them according to the **AGLC** is essential for reading and writing.

lessons.title: Definition and functions of tones
lessons.anelcac: Tones — definition, function, presentation; simple tones (high, low, mid)
objectives: Define tone as a distinctive feature of tone languages
Distinguish lexical tone from grammatical tone
Identify the simple tones of Bàsàa
Transcribing words with their tones according to AGLC

teacher.intro: Lesson: Definition and function of tones. Module: Module III — Suprasegmental phonology: tones.
steps: **Setting the context:** Say two Bàsàa words that are written the same but have different tones and different meanings.
**Presentation:** Define tone. Present the simple tones of Bàsàa and their AGLC diacritics.
**Explanation:** Simple tones: high (´), low (`), mid (¯). Have students repeat each tone.
**Application:** Match recorded words with their tone notation.
**Assessment:** Dictation of 5 words — students note the tones.
teacher.freedom: Singing the tones helps to memorise them. Use a flute or whistle the tonal melodies.
teacher.tips: Singing the tones helps to memorise them. Use a flute or whistle the tonal melodies.

student.intro: Bàsàa is a tonal language: the pitch of your voice changes the meaning of the word! You will learn to hear and write down these tones.
activities: Listen to the pairs of words. For each pair, are the tones the same or different?
Transcribe 5 words with their tones using the AGLC diacritics (´ ` ¯).
Find 2 words in the vocabulary that differ only in tone. What does each one mean?
Sing the tones of a 3-syllable word as High-Low-High, then Low-High-Low. What difference do you hear?
Memorise: high tone = ´ ; low tone = ` ; mid tone = ¯.
student.memo: In **Bàsàa**, tone is phonological: it distinguishes words with different meanings. The **simple tones** are high (´), low (`), and sometimes mid (¯). They are written using the **AGLC** diacritics.

lessons.title: Complex tones and tone-marked written production
lessons.anelcac: Complex tones (rising, falling); finding the tone of a word; tonal written production
objectives: Identify the complex tones of Bàsàa (rising, falling)
Finding the tone of a word by the isolation method
Transcribing sentences with full tone marking
Producing a short text in Bàsàa with correct tones

teacher.intro: Lesson: Complex tones and tonal written production. Module: Module III — Suprasegmental phonology: tones.
steps: **Setting the context:** Recall the simple tones. Announce that some syllables carry two tones in succession.
**Presentation:** Complex tones: falling (̂), rising (̌). Let students hear them and reproduce them.
**Explanation:** Isolation method: say the word with an artificial high tone, then a low one, and listen to which sounds natural.
**Application:** Students find the tone of 10 words in Bàsàa using the isolation method.
**Production:** Dialogue of 6 lines in Bàsàa with complete tone notation.
teacher.freedom: The complex falling tone is often the most frequent. Start with it before the rising tone.
teacher.tips: The complex falling tone is often the most frequent. Start with it before the rising tone.

student.intro: You know the simple tones. Now for the complex tones of Bàsàa — syllables that rise and fall at the same time!
activities: Listen to the recorded words and sort them: Simple tone | Complex tone.
Apply the isolation method to 5 words: say them high, then low, and note the tone you perceive.
Transcribe a dialogue of 4 lines in Bàsàa with all the tones marked.
Write a 3-sentence text in Bàsàa about an action from your daily life, with tone marking.
Memorise: falling tone = ̂ ; rising tone = ̌.
student.memo: The **complex tones** of **Bàsàa** (falling ̂, rising ̌) are melodic movements on a single syllable. The **isolation method** makes it possible to find the tone of an unknown word. A transcription in Bàsàa without tones is incomplete.

lessons.title: The noun base and noun classes
lessons.anelcac: NP: constituents, base noun + affixes, noun classes, personal pronouns
objectives: Identify the structure of the noun in Bàsàa (base + affixes)
Recognising the noun classes of Bàsàa
Form the singular and plural of nouns
Use the personal pronouns corresponding to noun classes

vocabulary.langText: à bê à gwèé ŋ̀ɔ́ ŋ̀kɛ́ŋí nì ǹtàndáá ú jɔ́ɔ́
vocabulary.frenchText: he had a big head and a long neck

vocabulary.langText: à yè nì màsɔ̀ŋ má máhíndí

teacher.intro: Lesson: The noun base and noun classes. Module: Module IV — The noun phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a noun in Bàsàa in the singular and plural. What changes?
**Presentation:** Noun class: in Bantu and Bantoid languages, nouns are grouped into classes marked by prefixes.
**Explanation:** Main noun classes of Bàsàa with singular and plural prefixes.
**Application:** Table: singular → plural for 10 nouns.
**Assessment:** Identify the noun class of 5 nouns.
teacher.freedom: Start from the nouns that students already use. Noun classes often correspond to semantic categories (humans, animals, objects…).
teacher.tips: Start from the nouns that students already use. Noun classes often correspond to semantic categories (humans, animals, objects…).

student.intro: In Bàsàa, nouns are organised into **classes**. Each class has its own prefixes for the singular and plural — a much richer system than gender in French!
activities: Using the Bàsàa vocabulary, make a table: Singular | Plural | Noun class.
Identify the class prefix in each noun. Highlight it.
Put the following 5 nouns into the plural by changing the prefix according to the class.
Match each noun with its corresponding class pronoun.
Memorise: **noun class** = grammatical category of nouns, marked by prefixes.
student.memo: In **Bàsàa**, nouns are organised into **noun classes** marked by prefixes. A change of prefix indicates number. Pronouns, adjectives and verbs agree with the class of the noun.

lessons.title: Noun determiners
lessons.anelcac: Determiners: possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives; noun class agreement
objectives: Identify the different types of determiners in Bàsàa
Make determiners agree with the noun according to the noun class
Build complex noun phrases
Producing sentences with complete NPs

vocabulary.langText: à bê à gwèé ŋ̀ɔ́ ŋ̀kɛ́ŋí nì ǹtàndáá ú jɔ́ɔ́
vocabulary.frenchText: he had a big head and a long neck

vocabulary.langText: à yè nì màsɔ̀ŋ má máhíndí

teacher.intro: Lesson: Noun determiners. Module: Module IV — The noun phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a simple noun phrase. How can it be enriched?
**Presentation:** Determiners in Bàsàa: possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives.
**Explanation:** Each determiner agrees with the class of the noun (same class prefix or suffix).
**Application:** Complete noun phrases with the correct determiner according to the class.
**Production:** 5 complex noun phrases (noun + 2 determiners) used in sentences.
teacher.freedom: Stress class agreement — one of the most distinctive features of Bàsàa compared with French.
teacher.tips: Stress class agreement — one of the most distinctive features of Bàsàa compared with French.

student.intro: A noun with its determiners becomes much more precise! In Bàsàa, determiners agree with the **noun class**.
activities: Complete the NPs with the correct possessive determiner according to the noun class.
Underline the determiners in 5 sentences in Bàsàa and identify their type.
Turn each simple noun phrase into a complex noun phrase by adding a demonstrative and a numeral.
Write 5 sentences in Bàsàa with at least two determiners per noun phrase.
Memorise: **class agreement** = the determiner changes form according to the noun class.
student.memo: In **Bàsàa**, all determiners (possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives) agree with the **noun class** of the noun. A **complex NP** = noun + nominal base + agreeing determiners.

lessons.title: The verb stem and conjugation
lessons.anelcac: VP: constituents, stem, affixes, conjugation, verb tenses
objectives: Identify the verb stem and the conjugation affixes in Bàsàa
Conjugate a verb in the main tenses
Analyse the morphological structure of a verb form
Use verb forms correctly in sentences

teacher.intro: Lesson: The verb stem and conjugation. Module: Module V — The verb phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a verb form in Bàsàa and ask students to identify the stem.
**Presentation:** Break down a verb form: subject prefix + TAM markers + stem + suffixes.
**Explanation:** Conjugation paradigm of a common verb in Bàsàa in several tenses.
**Application:** Conjugation table: 3 common verbs.
**Assessment:** Translate 5 sentences from French into Bàsàa.
teacher.freedom: The TAM system of Bàsàa is often richer than that of French. Start with the most commonly used tenses.
teacher.tips: The TAM system of Bàsàa is often richer than that of French. Start with the most commonly used tenses.

student.intro: The verb is the heart of the sentence in Bàsàa. It alone carries tense, aspect, mood and subject! In this lesson, you take apart the verbal mechanics.
activities: Break down 5 verb forms in Bàsàa: subject prefix | TAM marker | stem | suffix.
Conjugate the verb 'to eat' in Bàsàa in 3 different tenses for all persons.
Identify the tense of 5 sentences in Bàsàa and justify your answer.
Translate 3 sentences from French into Bàsàa, taking care with the conjugation.
Memorise: **TAM** = Tense-Aspect-Mood; this is what verbal affixes express in Bàsàa.
student.memo: In **Bàsàa**, a verb form = subject prefix + TAM markers + stem + suffixes. The **TAM** (Tense-Aspect-Mood) system expresses more precise temporal and aspectual nuances than in French.

lessons.title: Verbal moods and negation
lessons.anelcac: Moods: indicative, imperative; negation; written production of simple/complex VP
objectives: Identify and use the main verbal moods of Bàsàa
Form the verbal negation
Build simple and complex verb phrases
Producing a text with a variety of moods and aspects

teacher.intro: Lesson: Verbal moods and negation. Module: Module V — The verb phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Give an order in Bàsàa. Which mood is used?
**Presentation:** Moods in Bàsàa: indicative, imperative, and other aspectual moods.
**Explanation:** Formation of the negative in Bàsàa: prefix, negative suffix, or particle.
**Application:** Turn 5 affirmative sentences into negative ones and vice versa.
**Production:** 8-sentence text alternating affirmation, negation and imperative.
teacher.freedom: Negation in Bàsàa can be double (framing the verb) or simple. Show both cases.
teacher.tips: Negation in Bàsàa can be double (framing the verb) or simple. Show both cases.

student.intro: Giving an order, expressing doubt, denying an action — each nuance has its own form in Bàsàa!
activities: Put the 5 given sentences into the negative form.
Turn these 5 statements into imperatives addressed to a friend.
Identify the mood and polarity (affirmative/negative) of each sentence in the text provided.
Write a dialogue of 6 lines including at least 2 imperatives and 2 negations.
Memorise: **mood** = the way of viewing the action; **negation** = grammatical marker denying the action.
student.memo: In **Bàsàa**, the main moods are the **indicative** and the **imperative**. **Negation** is marked by a particle or a specific affix. The diversity of moods is an expressive richness of Bàsàa.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module VI — The sentence in Bàsàa
lessons.title: The simple sentence and its types
lessons.anelcac: Simple, interrogative, negative and imperative sentence; word order
objectives: Analyse the structure of the simple sentence in Bàsàa
Distinguish the 4 types of sentences
Mastering the order of constituents
Producing varied simple sentences

teacher.intro: Lesson: The simple sentence and its types. Module: Module VI — The sentence in Bàsàa.
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a sentence in Bàsàa. Who does what?
**Presentation:** Basic constituent order in Bàsàa. Compare with French.
**Explanation:** The 4 sentence types from the same basic sentence.
**Application:** Turn declarative sentences into interrogative ones, then into negative ones.
**Production:** 8 varied sentences (2 per type) about school life.
teacher.freedom: Word order in Bàsàa may differ from French. This is a typological feature, not a mistake.
teacher.tips: Word order in Bàsàa may differ from French. This is a typological feature, not a mistake.

student.intro: A well-constructed sentence in Bàsàa follows precise rules. You learn the types of sentences and word order.
activities: Identify the order of constituents in 5 sentences in Bàsàa.
Turn 4 declarative sentences into yes/no questions.
Turn these 4 sentences into negatives.
Write 2 sentences of each type (declarative, interrogative, negative, imperative).
Memorise: the basic order in **Bàsàa** is typologically stable.
student.memo: The **simple sentence** in **Bàsàa** has a characteristic order of constituents. The 4 types (declarative, interrogative, negative, imperative) are formed with specific grammatical markers.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module VI — The sentence in Bàsàa
lessons.title: Logical connectors and the complex sentence
lessons.anelcac: Logical connectors, complex sentence, coordination, subordination; written production
objectives: Identify the logical connectors of Bàsàa
Distinguish coordination from subordination
Build complex sentences
Producing a coherent text with syntactic variety

teacher.intro: Lesson: Logical connectors and the complex sentence. Module: Module VI — The sentence in Bàsàa.
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a short story in Bàsàa. Which words link the sentences?
**Presentation:** Connectors in Bàsàa: coordinating and subordinating conjunctions.
**Explanation:** Complex sentence by coordination / by subordination. Examples in Bàsàa.
**Application:** Link 5 pairs of simple sentences with the appropriate connector.
**Production:** 10-sentence text on 'A day in my village' with 5 different connectors.
teacher.freedom: The connectors of Bàsàa often have French equivalents but with different syntactic positions.
teacher.tips: The connectors of Bàsàa often have French equivalents but with different syntactic positions.

student.intro: To tell stories and argue, you need to link your sentences. The **logical connectors** of Bàsàa are your tools!
activities: Underline all the connectors in the text provided.
Classify them: Addition | Cause | Consequence | Opposition | Time.
Link 5 pairs of sentences with the most appropriate connector.
Write a text of 8 sentences with at least 4 different connectors.
Memorise: coordination = same level; subordination = one sentence inside another.
student.memo: In **Bàsàa**, **logical connectors** make it possible to build coherent **complex sentences**. Varying syntactic structures improves the quality of written and spoken expression.

lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and interacting in Bàsàa
lessons.anelcac: Everyday communication situations: greetings, introductions, polite expressions
objectives: Mastering greeting formulas according to context
Introducing yourself and someone else in Bàsàa
Use polite and respectful expressions
Holding a short everyday conversation

teacher.intro: Lesson: Greeting, introducing yourself and interacting in Bàsàa. Module: Module VII — Everyday life (Level 1).
steps: **Setting the context:** Two students meet at the market. Act out the scene in French, then ask how to say it in Bàsàa.
**Presentation:** Greetings in Bàsàa according to the time of day, age and context.
**Explanation:** Formulas of respect towards elders, specific to Bàsàa culture.
**Role play:** In groups of 2, simulate encounters in various contexts (market, school, ceremony).
**Production:** Dialogue of 10 lines between two people of different generations.
teacher.freedom: Greeting rules reflect deep cultural values. Value the knowledge of students from families who speak the language.
teacher.tips: Greeting rules reflect deep cultural values. Value the knowledge of students from families who speak the language.

student.intro: Knowing how to greet in Bàsàa means respecting the culture! The greetings change depending on whom you greet and at what time.
activities: Complete the table of Bàsàa greetings: Time | Formula | Expected response.
Play role A: greeting an elder at the morning market.
Make up a dialogue of 8 lines between a child and their grandfather.
Note down 3 Bàsàa politeness formulas with no direct equivalent in French.
Memorise the morning and evening greeting formulas, and those for elders, in Bàsàa.
student.memo: **Greetings** in **Bàsàa** vary according to the time of day, status and social context. They reflect the community's values of respect and solidarity.

lessons.title: Express everyday needs and actions
lessons.anelcac: Real-life situations: shopping, requests for help, travelling, daily activities
objectives: Express everyday needs in Bàsàa
Describe daily activities
Use vocabulary for places and actions of everyday life
Producing a descriptive text on a typical day

teacher.intro: Lesson: Expressing everyday needs and actions. Module: Module VII — Everyday life (Level 1).
steps: **Setting the context:** Images of scenes from daily life — market, field, school, home. How can they be described in Bàsàa?
**Presentation:** Thematic vocabulary: food, travel, household activities.
**Simulation:** Market scene: buyer and seller in Bàsàa.
**Application:** Describe your day in Bàsàa (from waking up to going to bed).
**Production:** 10-sentence text: 'My day in Bàsàa'.
teacher.freedom: Everyday vocabulary is the most motivating. Link the ALCAM words to real situations.
teacher.tips: Everyday vocabulary is the most motivating. Link the ALCAM words to real situations.

student.intro: You know how to greet people. Now you are going to manage in everyday situations in Bàsàa: at the market, on the road, at home.
activities: Match each picture of a scene from daily life with the corresponding word or sentence in Bàsàa.
Play the role of the seller at the market: answer the requests in Bàsàa.
Write 5 sentences describing your morning activities from the time you wake up.
Translate these 5 sentences about daily journeys into Bàsàa.
Memorise 10 everyday words in Bàsàa with their French translation.
student.memo: The **everyday** vocabulary in **Bàsàa** covers food, getting around and household activities. Mastering it allows functional communication in all contexts.

lessons.title: Argue and persuade in Bàsàa
lessons.anelcac: Elaborate communication: argumentation, narration, formal speech
objectives: Build a simple argument in Bàsàa
Use the expressions of formal speech
Narrating a past event coherently
Delivering a 2-minute oral speech in Bàsàa

teacher.intro: Lesson: Arguing and persuading in Bàsàa. Module: Module VIII — Everyday life (Level 2).
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a proverb in Bàsàa. Ask students to explain it and defend it.
**Presentation:** Formulas of formal oral speech in Bàsàa: forms of address, opening, closing.
**Explanation:** Structure of an argument: thesis → arguments → examples → conclusion.
**Practice:** Debate: for or against the use of Bàsàa at school? Each group defends its position.
**Production:** 2-minute speech on a given theme.
teacher.freedom: Public speaking is highly valued in Cameroonian cultures. Draw on this tradition to motivate the students.
teacher.tips: Public speaking is highly valued in Cameroonian cultures. Draw on this tradition to motivate the students.

student.intro: In Bàsàa cultures, well-spoken words are a force. You learn to argue and persuade with eloquence.
activities: Identify in the text: thesis, arguments, examples.
Prepare 3 arguments to defend the teaching of Bàsàa in primary school.
Give an opening speech for a ceremony in Bàsàa.
Narration: tell in Bàsàa about a memorable event from your school life.
Memorise the opening and closing formulas of a formal speech in Bàsàa.
student.memo: **Argumentation** in **Bàsàa** follows this pattern: thesis → arguments → examples → conclusion. **Formal speech** follows precise cultural conventions. Mastery of elaborate oral expression is a high-level skill.

lessons.title: Oral literature and advanced written production
lessons.anelcac: Oral literature: proverbs, tales, riddles; long written production
objectives: Analyse the structure of a tale or a riddle in Bàsàa
Identify the themes and values conveyed
Writing a short tale following the conventions of the genre
Using oral literature as a teaching resource

steps: **Setting the context:** Tell or play a short tale in Bàsàa.

**Application:** Analyse a tale provided, following this structure.
**Production:** Tale of at least 15 lines in Bàsàa with an explicit moral.
teacher.freedom: Oral literature is a threatened cultural treasure. Invite community storytellers if possible.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Central, majority group, part of a larger whole: the Lìmùù, Liŋgɔ̀k and Mbamndân have given up their own speech in favour of bàsàa. • The same speech variety is found throughout the Nyong-et-Kéllé and, with few variations, in the Sanaga-Maritime. • The group is homogeneous but strictly practises exogamy: the Ndog-Bacek do not marry among themselves. • The group occupies its ancestral land, which belongs to it; the place has no particular religious value. • The migration started from Ŋgɔk-Lituɓa, with a stop at Mbɔgkanda-Maholo; no ties have been kept with these places.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Ndog-Bacek form the majority core of a Basaa group that has absorbed several neighbouring groups (Lìmùù, Liŋgɔ̀k, Mbamndân), who adopted Bàsàa. Settled on their ancestral land after a migration that set out from Ŋgɔk-Lituɓa, they live mainly from cocoa, the oil palm and bananas, in a patrilineal society where decisions are taken by consensus.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “An important decision has to be made for the whole village of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). Who decides, and how?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Social organisation is based on caste and lineages. • Joint decisions are taken behind closed doors, by consensus, among the representatives of each family stock. • Interactions are open: the society describes itself as very democratic. • A sub-clan alliance bond between brothers and sisters, called lìɓàba, structures solidarity. • Tensions with neighbours are defused by purification rites (Sày-Tuggwêt), so that there is no resentment inherited from history.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “Your older brother wants to marry a young Basaa woman (Ndog-Bacek). Which steps will he have to follow?” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family, and frequent comings and goings to her parents' home are frowned upon. • One becomes a man by presenting one's fiancée to one's parents; one becomes a woman by presenting one's fiancé. No fixed age is required for marriage. • Stages: marriage request, bride price, then sealing of the union (ndombol likil). • The bride price comprises palm wine, kola, a goat and a wrapper: the wine erases the hardships of upbringing and brings cheer, the kola symbolises sharing and awakening, the goat “wipes away the blood” of the young woman's birth, the wrapper places her family under honour.

activities.instruction: Choose the most representative dance: participants, instruments, attire, gestures.

activities.title: I understand
activities.instruction: Explain whether it is a dance of joy, mourning, initiation or war.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), the traditional dances (mɓehla, hoŋgo, makunɛ) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: ŋgɔm, makwa, mandum, miŋkeŋ.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek)
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: traditional economy
objectives: Identify economic activities
Explain the division of tasks
Explain access to land
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). First you need to understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A development project wants to help the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). First, we need to understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men: cocoa farming, palm groves, banana plantations, livestock. Women: food crops (groundnut, cocoyam, cassava) and trade. • Land belongs to men; it is accessed through inheritance, bequest or purchase according to customary law. • Ancestral crafts: fishing net (tan), bed (likondo), bench (koma), hunting lamp (pɛn), game bag (hikamba).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: cocoa growing, oil-palm groves, banana plantations, livestock rearing. Women: food crops (groundnut, cocoyam, cassava) and trade. Land belongs to men; it is acquired by inheritance, bequest or purchase according to customary law.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Make a two-column table (men / women) of the activities of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I propose

student.memo: Men: cocoa growing, oil-palm groves, banana plantations, livestock rearing. Women: food crops (groundnut, cocoyam, cassava) and trade. Land belongs to men; it is acquired by inheritance, bequest or purchase according to customary law.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek)
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: symbolism, rites, taboos
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
Identify sacred places
Explain the role of taboos
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). Which places and rules must they absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A visitor arrives among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). What places and rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The old cults (ancestors in November, sowing in March, harvests in February) are no longer practised. • Sacred site linked to water: Dipɓkɔɔɓôm, at Nkoumisé, on the bank of the river Lɔ̀bɛ́. • Birth is seen as the return of an ancestor; death as a return to the ancestors, or as the result of human wickedness or a punishment from the universe. • It is possible to make contact with the spirit of the dead in difficult moments of life. • Major taboos: incest (likaa), murder (mbàk), eating a forbidden animal (cǒs). Serious offences (hitting one's parents, killing) are punished by quarantine.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The old cults (ancestors in November, sowing in March, harvests in February) are no longer practised. Sacred site linked to water: Dipɓkɔɔɓôm, in Nkoumisé, on the bank of the Lɔ̀bɛ́ river.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) (3 places or rules to respect, with the reason for each).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Find out what the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Bàsàa
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
Introducing yourself
Counting from 1 to 10
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in sharing the kola nuts while counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “You are visiting a Basaa family (Ndog-Bacek). Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the kola nuts by counting.” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Bàsàa. • Greeting formulas: Mɛ nyega = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); Mɛ nyega a = morning greeting (one person); Ma nyega bee = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Pɔk / yada, Iɓa, Iaa, Ina, Itan. • The founding ancestor, Bacek (ɓa joy), bears a name with a double meaning: “may they exterminate” or “may they be exterminated”. • The Ndog-Bacek resemble the other “Ndog” groups (dress, cooking, crafts).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Bàsàa are the first steps towards communicating with the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). Polite expressions show the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Bàsàa.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Bàsàa are the first steps towards communicating with the Basaa (Ndog-Bacek). Polite expressions show the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
